title: Where's the post office? — asking for directions
goal: Ask for and understand directions in town — and install the mestnik (Locative), the place form, while accepting a fact as it is: every preposition drags along its own case.
bekal: say where things are with *v* and *na*, knowing the choice is mostly habit, not logic
tell *v šoli* (at school) from *v šolo* (to school) without thinking twice

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Oprostite, kje je pošta?
dialogs.intro: Budi is standing at an intersection in central Ljubljana with an envelope in his hand. He stops a passerby.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Excuse me, where's the post office?

lines.speaker: Mimoidoči:
lines.id: The post office? Over there, around the corner.

lines.speaker: Mimoidoči:
lines.text: Ne, pet minut peš. Greste naravnost, potem levo.
lines.id: No, five minutes on foot. Go straight, then left.
lines.literal: no, five of-minutes on-foot. you-go straight, then left.

lines.speaker: Mimoidoči:
lines.id: Yes, at the traffic lights you turn left.

lines.speaker: Mimoidoči:
lines.text: Pošta je na desni, poleg banke.
lines.id: The post office is on the right, next to the bank.
lines.literal: post is on right, beside bank-gen.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Odlično. In kje je najbližji bankomat?
lines.id: Great. And where's the nearest ATM?
lines.literal: excellent. and where is nearest ATM?

lines.speaker: Mimoidoči:
lines.text: Prav pred pošto. Ne morete zgrešiti.
lines.id: Right in front of the post office. You can't miss it.
lines.literal: right in-front-of post-ins. not you-can miss.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Najlepša hvala! Lep dan še naprej!
lines.id: Thank you so much! Have a nice day!
lines.literal: most-beautiful thanks! nice day still onward!

notes: **Every preposition drags along its own case.** Just look at this one dialogue: *za vogalom* and *pred pošto* use one form, *pri semaforju* another, *poleg banke* and *do semaforja* a third. This isn't chaos — every preposition has a fixed partner, and the partner never changes. The full table is on the next page; learn each preposition **together** with its form, never on its own.

**Na pošti, but v trgovini.** Some places take *v* (in), some take *na* (on/at). Post offices, banks, universities, stations, and markets take *na*; shops, schools, cafés, and hospitals take *v*. Some of it can be explained by history — places that were once open spaces take *na* — but mostly it's just habit to be accepted. Learn them in pairs, much as English says "at the station" but "in the shop".

**Peš = on foot.** One word, no verb. *Grem peš* (I'm walking), *pet minut peš* (five minutes on foot). To ride something, Slovenian uses *z*: *z avtobusom*, *z avtom* — that form is installed in unit 18.

**Ne morete zgrešiti** literally "you can't miss (it)" — exactly like English "you can't miss it", and one of the most common ways Slovenians end a set of directions. If you hear it, the place you're looking for is big and obvious.

**Lep dan še naprej!** literally "nice day further on" — a goodbye to a stranger who has helped you, roughly "have a nice day". It sounds warm without being familiar, which is the right tone for someone you met thirty seconds ago.

grammars.title: Mestnik — the place form
body: This form only ever appears after a preposition, never on its own — that's why it's called *mestnik*, "the place case" (Locative). Its pattern is the easiest of all the cases: **-i** for feminine words, **-u** for masculine and neuter words.
after: Two other prepositions use the same form: **pri** (near, at someone's place) and **po** (along, after). *Pri semaforju* (at the traffic lights), *pri Maji* (at Maja's), *po kosilu* (after lunch).
*Pri* is very useful and has no single English equivalent: it means "near", "at someone's place", and "during". *Pri zdravniku* = at the doctor's. *Pri nas* = at our place, in our country.

grammars.title: Prepositions and their partner cases
body: This table is a map of the whole Slovenian case system on one page. You don't need to memorize it now; you need to **know it exists**, so the forms that turn up in later units don't feel random.

head: Preposition
Meaning
Case
Example
rows: **z / s, pred, za, nad, pod, med**

after: Rows three and five show the most important pair for daily life: **v** and **na** are used twice, and the case is what changes the meaning. *Grem v šol**o*** = I'm going to school (moving). *Sem v šol**i*** = I'm at school (staying).
This is why Slovenian needs six cases and not three: there are too few prepositions for everything people want to say, so the noun form shoulders part of the load.

grammars.title: Kje in kam — a pair you must keep apart
body: In English, "at school" and "to school" share the same noun and only the preposition changes. In Slovenian, the preposition is the **same** and it's the noun ending that changes.

head: Kje? (at rest)
Kam? (moving)
Meaning
rows: at the post office / to the post office
in the shop / to the shop

after: Notice that **the preposition doesn't help you at all** in the first four rows: *v* is used for both. The only thing marking direction is one letter at the end: *-i* for staying, *-o* for moving.

The fifth row is different because it involves a person: to go **to someone's place**, Slovenian uses *k* — *k zdravniku* (to the doctor's), *k mami* (to mom's). This form is called the dajalnik (Dative), and you'll meet it again in unit 15.

blocks.text: Learn every place **together with its preposition**. The third column is what will actually come out of your mouth; the first column is just the dictionary form.

Ljubljana is small, and two places serve as landmarks for everyone: **Tromostovje** (the Triple Bridge) in the city center, and **Ljubljanski grad** (Ljubljana Castle) on the hill you can see from everywhere. If you get lost, *Kje je Tromostovje?* will bring you back to the center from anywhere.

Notice **cerkev** → *v cerkvi*: the *e* in the last syllable vanishes as soon as an ending is added, just as happened with the adjective *svetel* → *svetla* in unit 4. The *e* that disappears is always a schwa.
The words below cover almost every direction you'll hear. The rest are place names, which you can always point to on a map.

*Izgubil sem se* and *Izgubila sem se* are your first peek at the past tense: the ending changes according to the gender of the **speaker**, not the listener. A woman says *izgubila*, a man *izgubil* — said **eez-GOO-beew**, because a final *l* always turns into *u*. The whole system is installed in unit 12.

blocks.title: Habits that help in Slovenia
items: Slovenians almost always stop when asked for directions, and very often walk you a few steps of the way. Don't be surprised.
If you start with *Oprostite, ali govorite angleško?*, many will answer in very good English — but if you stick with Slovenian, almost all of them will slow down and see you through to the end.
Distances in Slovenia are short. "Far" to someone from Ljubljana usually means a twenty-minute walk.
